paper_title: What It Is, Not What It Says: Securing Agentic Browsing Interactions with Web Semantics

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents increasingly browse the web on users' behalf, yet they consume webpages as screenshots or text, exposing their LLMs to unvetted third-party content. Browsers enforce semantics under which what an element can do depends on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Agents flatten these semantics, so injected text can persuade the LLM to exercise the user's authority for content that has none. As LLMs remain easy to persuade, the agent's interface to the web must itself ensure the integrity of what the agent reads, interprets, and does. We propose Intact, which runs on an unmodified browser. Intact builds GenTree, a bespoke representation that captures provenance and web semantics. Intact passes the page via GenTree to the LLM one element at a time, so the LLM decides on each element without any other element's text. Its harness executes each step only within the capabilities of the step's element and asks the user before acting on third-party content. On 1,270 real webpages, GenTree attributes 2.3x as many elements to third parties as the browser, which misattributes 58.7% of them to the first party. On 1,091 of these webpages with injected attacks, only 12.8% of attacks get through Intact's planner, each at most as a consent request, against 73.1% for a conventional planner. Isolation disrupts functionality on only 3.7% of tasks, and a parallel schedule could remove most of its added latency.

What It Is, Not What It Says: Securing Agentic Browsing Interactions with Web Semantics Umar Iqbal Washington University in St. Louis AbstractAI agents increasingly browse the web on users behalf, yet they consume webpages as screenshots or text, exposing their LLMs to unvetted third-party content. Browsers enforce semantics under which what an element can do depends on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Agents flatten these semantics, so injected text can persuade the LLM to exercise the users authority for content that has none. As LLMs remain easy to persuade, the agents interface to the web must itself ensure the integrity of what the agent reads, interprets, and does. We propose INTACT, which runs on an unmodified browser. INTACT builds GENTREE, bespoke representation that captures provenance and web semantics. INTACT passes the page via GENTREE to the LLM one element at time, so the LLM decides on each element without any other elements text. Its harness executes each step only within the capabilities of the steps element and asks the user before acting on third-party content. On 1,270 real webpages, GENTREE attributes 2.3 as many elements to third parties as the browser, which misattributes 58.7% of them to the first party. On 1,091 of these webpages with injected attacks, only 12.8% of attacks get through INTACTs planner, each at most as consent request, against 73.1% for conventional planner. Isolation disrupts functionality on only 3.7% of tasks, and parallel schedule could remove most of its added latency. 1. Introduction AI agents increasingly act on users behalf, and the web gives them an API to nearly every online service. Agentic browsers (e.g., Comet [1], Claude in Chrome [2], and Gemini in Chrome [3]) and frameworks (e.g., Browser Use [4]) read pages, click, fill forms, and navigate across sites, often within the users authenticated sessions. This reach carries fundamental risk, as web content is unvetted. Pages are assembled at runtime by parties their operators neither control nor always know. Third parties appear on 92% of pages, and the median site among the top thousand includes 66 of them [5]. As third parties load further third parties, about half of websites render content they did not load themselves [6]. The web is accordingly among the largest attack surfaces in computing. Cross-site scripting has ranked among MITREs two most dangerous software weaknesses every year since 2020, and in 2025 SQL injection joined it at the top [7]. One would thus expect agents to interface with the web through carefully designed mechanisms. Instead, they simply consume page as screenshot or as text derived from its markup [8], [4], exposing the underlying LLM directly to unvetted content. LLMs are known to follow instructions embedded in such content, i.e., prompt injection [9], and to fall for scams [10]. Model-level defenses reduce but do not eliminate either [11], [12], [13], and OpenAI concedes that prompt injection, much like scams and social engineering on the web, is unlikely to ever be fully solved [14]. Such attacks are already manifesting in practice. Hidden instructions in Reddit posts and comments have led deployed agents to leak users one-time login codes and credit card numbers [15], [16], crafted links have made them exfiltrate email and calendar data [17], injected page elements and pop-ups divert web agents at high rates [18], [19], and injections aimed at agents appear on live websites [20], [21]. The key issue is that web markup was designed for rendering, not for agentic interfacing. Browsers invest considerable effort in enforcing its semantics. Each element has well-defined capabilities, and origins and frames bound what code from one party can do to another [22], [23], [24]. In the browser, what content can do thus depends on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Screenshots and text serializations flatten these semantics, leaving naturallanguage text that affords the LLM neither meaning nor control.

element cannot issue network request, yet its text can cause one by persuading the agent, which then acts as confused deputy [25], exercising the users authority for content that has none. Considering the well-known limitations of LLMs, we argue that security cannot rest on the models judgment; the interface between the web and the agent must itself ensure integrity [26], [27]. Input integrity requires knowing who created or modified each piece of content the agent reads. Processing integrity requires that no element lead the agent beyond what the element itself affords. Output integrity requires that every action, and the data flow it causes, be warranted by the users request and permitted by the webs security boundaries. All three must hold with little loss of functionality. In this paper, we address this problem with INTACT. Our key idea is to reuse the semantics that browsers already enforce and extend them with the provenance, capturing both in GENTREE, per-element representation of the page through which INTACT mediates what the agent reads, in1 terprets, and does. For input integrity, INTACT attributes every DOM creation and modification to the responsible script [28], [29] and taints what third parties create or modify. The browser does not make this distinction out of the box, because it attributes everything third-party script creates in page to the first-party context. For processing integrity, INTACT introduces virtual isolation, which extends the browsers enforcement of markup semantics to the agent without any change to the browsers architecture. INTACT passes content to the LLM one element at time, so an elements text never reaches the decision on another element, and each action the agent derives stays tied to the element it came from, whose properties INTACT can then enforce. The

above thus cannot cause request, whatever its text says. For output integrity, INTACT controls each action based on the provenance, capabilities, effects, and security boundaries of the elements involved. These checks depend only on the page, so INTACT can enforce them reliably. The users intent, however, is not encoded in the page, so INTACT defers to the user for decisions that the page cannot settle, e.g., using third-party booking widget that the task requires. INTACT thus need not recognize injected content as malicious or prevent the agent from being persuaded; it limits what persuaded agent can do. Our key contributions are as follows: 1) We propose and implement GENTREE, bespoke representation for AI agents that records the provenance and web semantics of every element. On tested webpages, GENTREE attributes 2.3 as many elements to third parties as the browsers standard attribution, which misattributes 58.7% of them to the first party. 2) We operationalize GENTREE in INTACT, virtual isolation architecture that runs on an unmodified browser. INTACT passes the page to the LLM one element at time and executes each step only within that elements capabilities under web semantics. What an element says thus cannot change what it can do. 3) We evaluate INTACT against VANILLA, conventional planner, on 1,091 real webpages. Only 12.8% of attacks get through INTACTs planner, each at most as request for user consent, against 73.1% for VANILLA. INTACT disrupts functionality on 3.7% of tasks, and parallel schedule could significantly reduce its time overhead. 4) To foster follow-up research, we release INTACTs source code and our attack benchmark of 1,091 real webpages at https://github.com/llm-platform-security/ intact. Looking ahead, we see GENTREE as substrate for existing agent defenses. For example, defenses based on execution isolation [30], controland data-flow enforcement [31], [32], and permission management [33] all presuppose knowing which inputs are untrusted and what each component can do, structure that webpages do not provide explicitly and that GENTREE derives automatically. 2. Background and Motivation 2.1. Overview of Agentic Browsers in which the agent AI agents that act on the web on users behalf are becoming increasingly prevalent. These range from native agentic browsers, such as Perplexitys Comet [1] and Dia [34], into the browser, to non-native agents, such as Browser Use [4] and SeeAct [8], that drive commodity browser through external automation, such as Playwright [35] and the Chrome DevTools Protocol [36]. Conventional browsers, such as Google Chrome [37] and Microsoft Edge [38], are also adding agentic features. is built At high level, agents perceive page through (i) textual representations derived from the DOM [39] and the accessibility tree [40], (ii) visual representations of the rendered page, or combination of both. With textual representation, the agents harness, i.e., the code around the LLM, attaches an identifier to each element, and the LLM names that identifier in its action, e.g., click [1582] in WebArena [41]. The harness then performs the action on that element, from within the browser in native agentic browsers or through the automation framework in non-native agents. With visual representation, the agent instead determines the on-screen coordinates at which to click or type [41]. 2.2. Security and Privacy Concerns These representations serve the agents functional needs but give little consideration to security and privacy. They reuse views built for other consumers, namely screenshots for people, the DOM for scripts, and the accessibility tree for assistive technologies. Once serialized, third-party advertisement and the sites own checkout button are both just text. These representations thus undo three of the webs protections: the isolation between origins, the defenses against content injection, and the human in the loop. First, the web isolates content from different origins. The same-origin policy keeps one origins code from reading or acting on another origins content [23], and site isolation enforces this boundary with separate processes [24]. representation that flattens the page into one text or one image erases these boundaries, so the LLM receives third partys content next to the sites own and has no reliable way to tell them apart. Once the agent follows instructions in that content, the same-origin policy and cross-origin resource sharing become, in Braves words, effectively useless [15]. the web has developed principled defenses against content injection. In cross-site scripting, an attacker injects markup that runs with the pages authority, and the web counters it by sanitizing untrusted input. Agents recast this attack in form that sanitization cannot catch. Injected plain text carries no executable markup, so it passes the sanitizer. Once an agent reads this text, however, its instructions can direct the agent to perform, with the users authority, the actions that sanitization denies to injected scripts [9]. Second, 2 Third, the webs security model counts on human behind each action. Browsers gate sensitive operations, such as opening pop-ups, behind user activation [22], ask the user before site may use the camera or location, and show the sites origin in the address bar. These checks presume that the user performs each action and sees each page, which no longer holds when an agent drives the browser. These weaknesses are serious because LLMs are now capable enough to act on their own, yet remain easy to mislead. For example, when researchers asked Comet to buy an Apple Watch from fake Walmart store, in some runs, Comet filled in the saved address and card details without asking for confirmation and completed the purchase within seconds [10]. LLMs also err without an attacker [41], and model-level defenses make them harder to persuade but not reliable [11], [12], [13]. The agents integrity therefore depends on oversight of what goes into the LLM, what the LLM can do with it, and which actions it proposes as result, i.e., of the LLMs input, processing, and output [26], [27]. This oversight must happen outside the LLM, in code that page content cannot persuade. 2.3. Key Idea and Challenges Our key idea is that the browser already has the information that this oversight needs. The browser parses every element and enforces its semantics, e.g., link navigates and form submits its fields, whereas

element can do neither [22]. It knows the origin and frame of every document [23], and it runs every script that creates or modifies an element. We capture this information as the page loads and expose it to the agents harness in GENTREE, bespoke representation for agentic interactions that records, for every element, who created or modified it and what it can do. We do not rely on websites to author such representation, because sites adopt even established security mechanisms slowly and incompletely, as with Content Security Policy [42]. Building GENTREE and using it for oversight raise three challenges, one each for the LLMs input, processing, and output. 2.3.1. Input Integrity. The first challenge is to know who created or modified each element, which input integrity requires. Under our threat model (3), injected instructions enter the page through third party, such as script, frame, or feed. defense can therefore track this untrusted input as taint rather than inspect content for malice, as defenses against cross-site scripting do [43]. Out of the box, however, the browser attributes what third-party script writes into the first-party document to the first party, and this standard attribution misses 58.7% of third-party elements on the pages that we crawled (as we find in 5.2). Defenses that build on this attribution inherit its gap. Chromes agent, for example, hides frames whose origins are unrelated to the task [37], but content that third-party script writes into the first-party document carries the first partys origin and passes this check, so the agent treats it as the sites own. Recent research defenses do not record authorship either [44], [45]. For example, Untrusted Content Masking (UCM) has the site owner, or an LLM, label the regions that hold untrusted content [44], and Prismata has an LLM infer which kind of party authored each element, e.g., the sites developer, its users, or an external party, from cues in the markup [45]. Content that third-party script writes into the first-party document thus counts as the sites own unless label or cue gives it away, so these defenses address input integrity only in part. Further, site owner cannot label all such content, because webpages are dynamic. That is, third-party scripts create and modify elements at runtime, and the owner neither controls nor always knows what they write or load. Moreover, labels that an LLM infers rest on the LLMs judgment, which brings back the very problem that input integrity should solve. We instead build on prior work on browser instrumentation that records how scripts construct page [28], [29], [46], attributing every DOM creation and modification to the responsible script and tainting what third parties create or modify, without relying on any LLM (4.1.2). 2.3.2. Processing Integrity. The second challenge is to keep the content that the LLM reads from steering how the LLM processes the rest of the page. When the LLM reads the whole page at once, one elements text can direct an action on any other element, and the agent becomes confused deputy [25]. The attacker needs such an action, because its goal must exceed what its own element can do, or it would not need the agent. Prior defenses, such as UCM [44] and Prismata [45], still pass the page to one LLM that plans over it as whole, after they restrict the content that they consider untrusted, e.g., user reviews and advertisements. Whatever the labels miss thus still reaches an LLM that sees the whole page, and single mislabeled element raised UCMs attack success rate from 0% to 6%, close to the 8% of prompt-based defense [44]. Further, these defenses restrict the capabilities of untrusted content, whereas we find that third-party content provides useful functionality, such as links, forms, and text fields (Table 2) . We instead plan one element at time, third-party elements included, and the call that decides an element sees no other elements text (4.2). Each call can thus propose steps only on its own element, because our code, not the LLM, ties each proposed step to that element. Planning one element at time, however, raises challenge of its own, because step often depends on earlier steps, e.g., after query is typed, the next step is the search button. To address this, we pass log of the operations decided so far, without the text of any other element. Our intuition is that capable LLM needs to know only what the plan has done so far, not what other elements say. Still, this limited context can disrupt some tasks, so we measure how much functionality isolation costs (5.4). 2.3.3. Output Integrity. The third challenge is to decide what the agent may do on each element. The harness executes step only if, under web semantics, the element affords the steps operation. For example, the harness rejects 3 click on heading that sits outside any link or button, whatever the heading says. Deriving these capabilities is non-trivial, because neither the tag nor the accessibility tree always shows what an element does. An ARIA role can turn

into button, script rather than the tag defines custom elements behavior, and hidden input is absent from the accessibility tree yet is submitted with its form. To address this, we build taxonomy of capabilities that follows the HTML specification [22] and ARIA [40], i.e., the interactions that each element affords and the effects that they can have, and we label every element of GENTREE with it, accounting for the elements ancestors, ARIA attributes, and computed style (4.1). Further, web semantics cannot settle every step, e.g., whether to use third-party booking widget that the task requires, so some steps need the users consent. Asking about every step would defeat the purpose of an agent, but provenance and web semantics let the harness ask only about the riskiest steps, e.g., steps on thirdparty elements or steps with external effects. Together, these answers improve the security of the agent by design rather than by the LLMs judgment. 2.4. Complexity of Real Webpages We design INTACT and GENTREE to work on real webpages in practice, which are complex and which benchmarks struggle to replicate. For example, many parties assemble real page at runtime, they load further parties, embed services such as payment forms in cross-origin frames, and modify one anothers elements. Self-hosted pages lack the live third parties that make attribution hard and that tasks rely on, and few sites cannot show whether defense holds across the variety of the web. We therefore evaluate INTACT on real webpages captured with their live third-party content, 1,270 for attribution and 1,091 for attacks and functionality (5). We also release the 1,091 webpages with our attacks as benchmark. 3. Threat Model System Model. We consider an agent that autonomously interfaces with the web. The agent consists of an LLM and harness, i.e., the code around the LLM. The harness gives the LLM view of the page, e.g., its markup, and executes the LLMs decisions, such as clicking elements, filling in forms, and navigating. Webpages combine first-party content with third-party scripts, advertisements, and embedded services, which may appear directly in the first-party document or in cross-origin frames. Third-party content may originate from arbitrary sources and is not known to the user or the first-party operator in advance. Attacker Capabilities and Goals. We assume third-party attacker who controls some content on page that the agent visits, but has no special access to the user, the agent, or the first-party origin. The attacker may control only content, e.g., promotional note that an honest third partys script relays into the first-party document. It may run code in its own cross-origin frame, e.g., an embedded payment form. The attackers content may be hidden from view and still reach the agent. The attacker may target an element of the first party or of another third party (outbound attacks) or present its own elements as bait (inbound attacks). We consider attacks that require the agent, i.e., attacks that the attacker cannot carry out with its own capabilities.

element cannot carry out such an attack; script can, unless it runs inside crossorigin frame. We impose this condition because an attacker who can achieve its goal through its own scripts or content does not need the agent. Trust Relationships. We assume that the user, browser, and the agent harness are trustworthy and uncompromised. The LLM has no intent of its own to harm the user, but we do not trust its judgment. We assume that the attacker can persuade it to follow any instruction in the content that it reads, since model-level defenses reduce but do not eliminate prompt injection [11], [12], [13]. The LLM may also err without an attacker [41], [47]. We assume an honest first party and trust what its own responses and scripts deliver. We treat as untrusted all content in third-party frames, every element that third partys script creates or modifies, and every write whose script cannot be identified. Our instrumentation runs in the pages JavaScript environment, so we also assume that page scripts do not evade or tamper with it; moving the instrumentation into the browser would remove this assumption (6). Scope. Our goal is to prevent the attackers content from leading the agent to act beyond the users request, whether the content sits in the first-party document or in crossorigin frame. Concretely, the attackers text may reach the decisions on its own elements but no decision on another element. Every step must stay within its elements capabilities, and no step on third-party element may execute without the users consent. We consider the webpage on which the agent plans, not attacks that span several pages. Out of scope. We do not seek to detect or eliminate prompt injection; we aim to constrain its effects when the agent encounters untrusted content. We also exclude attackers who control the first-party origin itself. We do not address availability: an attacker can make the agent fail task, e.g., with decoy that draws the planner away from the part of the page that the task needs (6). 4. INTACT: System Architecture We propose INTACT, an execution architecture for secure agentic web interfacing. INTACTs main thesis is that the agents integrity depends on oversight of the LLMs input, processing, and output, as the LLM itself remains unreliable. INTACT bases this oversight on web semantics, i.e., on what each element is and where it comes from, not on what the element says. To oversee the input, INTACT builds GENTREE, bespoke representation of the page that records, for each element, which party created or modified it and what it can 4 do (4.1). To oversee the processing, INTACT plans under virtual isolation (4.2). It shows the LLM one element of GENTREE at time instead of the whole page, so the LLM decides on each element without any other elements text. The resulting plan carries little information beyond what the user asked for, yet it is directly actionable. To oversee the output, the harness (not the LLM) turns the plan into browser actions. It permits each step only within the capabilities of the element that the step names, and it asks the user before it acts on any third-party element. Figure 1 describes the execution flow in INTACT. We implement INTACT in Python on stock Chromium, which we drive through Playwright [35] and the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) [36]. We release our source code at https://github.com/llm-platform-security/intact. 4.1. GENTREE Construction To control what the LLM reads and what its decisions can cause, INTACT needs representation of the page in which this control can be expressed. Agents currently reuse representations built for other consumers, namely screenshots, the DOM, and the accessibility tree, which lend no such control (2.2). We create GENTREE, which extends these generic representations with the semantics that INTACT needs, so that each element carries what the harness requires to decide what that elements content may cause. GENTREE combines the DOM of every frame, the accessibility tree, and provenance into one record per element, which makes it much richer representation than any of the three alone (Figure 2). Each record holds the elements tag, attributes, direct text, and parent; the document it belongs to and whether that document is firstor third-party; its accessibility role and name, when the element is in the accessibility tree; its provenance, i.e., the script that created it, if any, and the parties that modified its attributes, text, or event listeners; and its capabilities.1 GENTREE also keeps the elements that the accessibility tree omits, such as scripts, hidden inputs, and hidden subtrees, because their content can still reach an agent. As each record already carries the elements provenance and capabilities, GENTREE also provides extensibility for fine-grained access control that may encode user preferences over them. 4.1.1. Web Semantics Representation. Provenance tells INTACT who created or modified an element, but not what that element can do. GENTREE thus also records each elements capabilities under the webs semantics, so that the harness can oversee the output. To that end, we create taxonomy of capabilities along two axes, following the the HTML specification [22] and ARIA semantics that define for each element: (i) the interactions that the element affords an agent, e.g., CLICK, TYPE, and UPLOAD (ten in total), and (ii) the effects that these interactions can have in the browser, e.g., NAVIGATE, SEND-REQUEST, and DOMMUTATE (thirteen in total). Effects are limited to observable 1. We identify party by its registrable domain (eTLD+1, computed with the Public Suffix List [48]). browser consequences; whether request amounts to, say, purchase is judgment that we leave to separate layer. We statically assign these labels from each elements tag and attributes with 76 rules, grouped by element family such as links, forms, media, embedded content, and dialogs, and 14 composition rules then adjust them for the elements ancestors, ARIA attributes, and computed style. For example, text inside link inherits the links CLICK, and disabled button loses all its interactions. GENTREE also records the channels through which an elements content reaches the agent, e.g., its text, accessible name, or placeholder. The taxonomy further records whether each effect can be undone. local change, such as DOM-MUTATE, can be reverted; an external effect, such as SEND-REQUEST, cannot be recalled once it occurs; and an undetermined effect, such as SUBMIT or NAVIGATE, has consequences that the label alone does not settle (Appendix lists the category of each effect). Typing into field of the first-party document is local change, or undetermined when the field sits in form, since typing can submit the form. Typing into field of third partys frame is an external effect, because that third party can read the value. Custom elements, whose behavior is defined by script rather than by the specification, cannot be labeled statically. GENTREE exposes their text but grants them no interactions unless an ARIA role declares one, e.g., role="button" confers CLICK; the harness therefore does not act on them otherwise, which favors safety over functionality. 4.1.2. Browser Instrumentation. GENTREEs provenance requires knowing which script, if any, created each element text, or event and which scripts modified its attributes, listeners, but the DOM records neither. The browser attributes everything that script writes into document to that documents origin, so content that third-party script injects into the first-party page is indistinguishable from the sites own, as with the button in Figure 2. We therefore instrument the browser to attribute every DOM creation and modification to the responsible script, which lets GENTREE separate what the site wrote from what third party injected into it. Before the page loads, we use CDP to register script that runs in every frame before the pages own scripts, wraps the DOM interfaces through which scripts create, insert, and modify elements, and attributes each call to the running script, which it reads from the JavaScript call stack. Script Identity. We identify script by its party, its URL, and the hash of its content, which CDP reports for every script that the JavaScript engine compiles, so that different scripts served from the same URL remain distinct. Code that has no URL of its own, i.e., code passed to eval or Function and inline scripts that another script inserts, would hide its origin from the call stack, so we give it synthetic source URL that maps back to the script that created it; the functions it defines, including callbacks that run later, such as timers, thus stay attributed through any chain of such indirections. We strip the source URLs that page code declares so that one script cannot pose as another. 5 Figure 1. Overview of INTACT. (1) As the browser loads the page, our instrumentation attributes every creation and modification of an element to the script responsible for it and taints what third parties create or modify (4.1.2). (2) INTACT then combines the DOM of every frame, the accessibility tree, and these attributions into GENTREE, labeling each element with its capabilities (4.1). (3) To plan task, INTACT shows the LLM one element at time and records the operation, if any, that the task needs on that element (4.2). (4) The harness executes the resulting plan, permitting each step only within the capabilities of the element it names. Amber marks third-party content, teal marks what our code adds, and violet marks the LLM. tion does not yet cover cookies, postMessage exchanges, content that browser extensions inject, or shadow roots, and it can be extended to them. Appendix gives further implementation details of the instrumentation. 4.2. Planning under Virtual Isolation GENTREE tells INTACT what each element is, but deciding what task requires still takes the LLMs judgment. INTACT therefore needs planning paradigm that keeps control and integrity with the harness, that the LLM cannot simply evade, and that still lets the agent carry out the users tasks. When the LLM reads the whole page at once, as agents do today, one elements text can redirect how the LLM treats every other element, and an action that it proposes cannot be traced to the content that prompted it. We instead iterate over GENTREE and show the LLM one element at time, which, for all intents and purposes, runs each element in isolation: its text can inform the decision about that element but no decision about another, which we refer to as virtual isolation. Planning one element at time raises the question of what context the LLM needs. Earlier elements are useful context, e.g., after query is typed, the next step is the search button, but passing their text would reintroduce the cross-element influence that isolation removes. We therefore pass the minimal context necessary (Figure 3): (i) the users request; (ii) the current elements own markup, i.e., its tag, fixed set of visible attributes (e.g., href, aria-label, placeholder, and type), and its direct text; (iii) log of the operations decided so far, each with the tag name of the element it was decided on, how many elements back that element is, and whether it shares the current elements form; and (iv) line that says whether the current element is inside form and how many elements back that form began. Our code derives the log and the form line from the pages structure, and neither carries text, attribute values, Figure 2. An abridged GENTREE record from our crawl, with its domains anonymized. An advertisers script created this button in the sites firstparty document. write whose script cannot be identified is marked as unattributed and treated as untrusted rather than as firstparty. Coverage. For each element, the wrappers record the script that created it, the script that inserted it, and the parties that set its attributes or text or attached event listeners to it. Interfaces that build elements from HTML strings, such as innerHTML and document.write, do not return the elements that they create, so we collect these elements with mutation observer that we read synchronously around the call. CDPs network events attribute each third-party request to the script that initiated it. Cross-origin frames, which Chromiums site isolation runs in separate processes [24], get their own CDP session and the same instrumentation, and are merged into the pages GENTREE. The instrumenta6 element by element until the form ends, which is the only way in which the walk crosses chunk boundary. Virtual isolation covers the calls that decide on elements, but two things that shape the walk lie outside it: (i) which chunk the walk covers and (ii) the log of earlier decisions. The relevance and choice calls read whole chunks, so text that an attacker injects can steer which chunk the planner walks, although these calls propose no step. The log reports the operations decided on earlier elements, including an attackers element, so the decision on that element can affect how later calls read their own elements, although the log carries none of its text. Neither input lets an elements text reach the decision on another element or name an element to act on. Instead, both let an attacker derail the plan, e.g., with decoy that draws the walk away from the part of the page that the task needs, which affects whether the task completes rather than what the agent may do; Section 6 discusses these attacks on availability. The output is plan, which is the ordered steps that the LLM marked as needed, each with the elements identifier, the operation, and the value (Figure 4). Extended Attribution via Instrumentation Input integrity rests on attribution, so we first measure how far GENTREE extends the browsers standard attribution. The remaining 1,017 take routes that VANILLAs plans do not, e.g., on TravelChinaGuide, INTACTs plan also types both cities into the sites search box and clicks several links to tour pages. The extra steps thus lengthen INTACTs plans, mostly without changing what the plans do. The judge finds the two plans equivalent, i.e., offering the same functionality, on three quarters of the tasks (811, 74.3%), different on 176 (16.1%), and uncertain on 104 (9.5%). It rates about as many plans of each planner appropriate, 613 of INTACTs (56.2%) and 647 of VANILLAs (59.3%), but rates INTACTs plans inappropriate twice as often, 109 (10%) against 54 (4.9%). The judge cannot decide on about third of each planners plans, 369 of INTACTs 13 Per Task VANILLA INTACT Ratio Model calls Input tokens Cached Output tokens Cost (US$) Time (s) 1 16,571 0 81 0.0021 2.5 55 50,152 25,560 3,796 0.0045 83. 55 2.8 45 2.1 34 Table 6: Planning cost per task. (33.8%) and 390 of VANILLAs (35.7%). Among the verdicts that it can decide, 85% of INTACTs plans and 92% of VANILLAs are appropriate. Both plans are appropriate on 538 tasks, only VANILLAs on 40, only INTACTs on ten, and neither on 23. Most uncertain verdicts concern what the page cannot show, chiefly what later page offers, and by the judges own reasons, 422 of its 759 uncertain verdicts on plans are uncertain only about later pages. Since the judge is the same model as the planners, sees neither operations nor values, and no step is executed, these verdicts assess the capabilities of the selected elements rather than task completion. By the judges measure, isolation thus costs functionality on few tasks, namely the 40 (3.7%) on which only VANILLAs plan is appropriate. Takeaway. Isolated planning is largely robust, losing functionality on only small share of tasks. Many of the steps that it misses are tangential to the task, such as answers to cookie dialogs that the task does not ask for. Planning with limited context, which withholds exactly the context that the attacks of Section 5.3 exploit, is thus promising direction for secure agents. 5.5. Overhead of Isolation INTACT may incur additional cost because of its design. Isolation adds overhead in other systems as well, such as site isolation in Chromium [24] and LLM-based systems [30]. Its planner decides on one element at time and therefore makes many more model calls than whole-page planning, so we measure this overhead. Deployability also depends on whether defense requires changes to the browser or cooperation from websites, which we discuss last. We measure the cost of planning the 1,091 benign tasks of Section 5.4 with INTACT and with VANILLA. Both planners use the same model; INTACTs planner runs its relevance checks four at time and then walks the chosen chunk one element after another. As the benchmark excludes the seven webpages on which INTACTs planning exceeded 15 minutes, these measurements miss the slowest webpages. The token counts include the simulation instruction of Section 5.3, which adds about 100 tokens to every call and which deployment would omit. 5.5.1. Results. Table 6 reports the medians, and Figure 7 their distributions over the tasks. INTACTs planner makes Figure 7. Planning cost and time per task. Each curve gives the fraction of the 1,091 tasks whose plan costs (a) or takes (b) at most the value on the x-axis, and dots mark the medians. The dashed curve estimates INTACTs time under parallel schedule. median of 55 calls per task, between 8 and 321, against VANILLAs single call. Per task, it reads 2.8 times as many input tokens as VANILLA, costs 2.1 times as much, and takes 34 times as long. Its median cost is $0.0045 against $0.0021, and its median time 83 seconds against 2.5. In absolute terms, isolation adds median of $0.0023 per task, about quarter of cent, and no plan costs more than $0.024. Isolation thus roughly doubles what task costs and makes planning much slower. The cost stays low because much of INTACTs input is cheap to serve. The relevance checks account for about 41% of it, since together they read the whole page in chunks, and the walk accounts for most of the rest. Each call of the walk begins with the same instructions and ten examples, which the provider caches, so 50% of INTACTs input tokens are served from its cache at discount, and the cost grows less than the tokens. INTACT also produces more output, median of 3,796 tokens against 81, since each of its calls returns its own decision. The time comes mostly from the walk, whose calls we make one after another, since each decision depends on the operations decided before it. Across the 1,091 tasks, linear fit shows that plans time grows by about 2.6 seconds for each element that the planner walks and 0.6 seconds for each chunk that it checks; by this fit, the walk accounts for about 76% of plans time, at the median over plans. Most of the latency thus comes from making the walks calls one at time. Isolation, however, requires one call per element, not one call at time, so running calls in parallel could remove most of this latency. The relevance checks are independent of each other, so they can all run at once. The walk can run in parallel as well, because 88% of the walked elements are not needed, and these decisions leave the log of operations unchanged. The planner can thus decide all of chunks elements at once and then decide again, with the updated log, only the elements that follow each newly decided step, so that every decision still sees exactly its element and the operations before it. Replaying the recorded decisions of all 1,091 walks, this schedule would shorten the critical path from median of 34 sequential calls to five, or from 83.2 seconds to 12.5 at each plans measured time per sequential call (a median of 2.5 seconds); it would add median of 14 26 calls for the elements decided again, about $0.0014 per task. parallel schedule would thus cut the median planning time by about 85% for small extra cost, without changing what any call sees. We have not implemented this schedule, and the estimate assumes that the model repeats its recorded decisions and that parallel calls take as long as sequential ones. In deployment, the remaining calls also overlap with the browsers own work, since the harness can execute each step once the planner has decided it and the checks have passed, while the planner decides on the next elements. Model calls already dominate the latency of deployed agents, for example on OSWorld, computer-use agents take tens of minutes for tasks that humans complete in few minutes, and large model calls for planning, reflection, and judging account for most of that time [51]. VANILLA, which plans page in single call, thus sets low bar for latency, and against agents that make several calls per page, the latency that INTACT adds is relatively smaller. Finally, INTACT requires neither changes to the browser nor cooperation from websites. It runs on stock Chromium, which it drives through Playwright and CDP (4), and registers its instrumentation as script that runs before the pages own scripts. Its planner uses an off-the-shelf model through standard chat API, without fine-tuning. Takeaway. Like other isolation systems, INTACT trades overhead for security, since planning one element at time raises the cost of task and slows planning down even more. As isolation does not require the calls to run one after another, parallel schedule could remove most of this latency without weakening security. 6. Discussion and Conclusion Attacks on Availability. While INTACT restricts what an attackers content can cause, the attacker can still target availability. For example, it may taint the whole page, or large sections of it, so that every step on them requires the users consent. To taint the sites own elements, however, the attacker must run script in the first-party document. Such script can read the page and act on it without the agent, which places the attacker outside our threat model (3). An attacker confined to its own content or frame can taint only elements of its own, which reduces this attack to decoy. Such decoy can draw the planner away from the part of the page that the task needs, by steering the calls that choose which chunk to walk (Section 4.2), or falsely halt the execution. For example, the planner may propose step on the decoy itself, such as click on Continue button that looks like the next step of form. Defending against such attacks on availability remains future work. Overheads. Isolation costs INTACT some functionality and adds cost and latency (5.4 and 5.5), but each of these overheads can be reduced. Our planner uses an off-theshelf model with few-shot examples. model fine-tuned to choose the chunk and decide on each element could recover many of the steps that INTACTs plans lack and avoid the extra steps that change nothing. The added latency also matters less than the comparison with VANILLA suggests, because tasks on the web take time regardless. The agent waits for each new page to load, and computer-use agents already take tens of minutes for tasks that people complete in few minutes [51]. Parallel schedules can reduce the latency further at the expense of cost. For example, the schedule of 5.5 would cut the median planning time by about 85%. smaller fine-tuned model could also lower the cost. Browser vs. JavaScript Instrumentation. We instrument from JavaScript, so our instrumentation runs with the same privileges as the pages own scripts, and page script could alter it. This risk stems from JavaScripts semantics rather than from our approach. We can move the same hooks into the browser, where page scripts cannot alter them, by extending prior in-browser instrumentation [28], [46], [52]. Prior work also shows that such instrumentation is practical. AdGraph adds only minor overhead to page loading [28], and VisibleV8 consistently outperforms equivalent instrumentation from JavaScript [52]. In-browser instrumentation must be carried forward through browser releases. However, VisibleV8s patches were maintained across ten Chrome versions without difficulty [52], and AI-assisted coding can ease this maintenance further, as it has for large code migrations [53]. Uses of GENTREE Beyond INTACT. GENTREE can serve uses beyond INTACT. Controlling the autonomy and access of agents remains an open problem, and different stakeholders may want to control them in different ways. user, for example, may want to automate routine decisions, as in systems that predict the users permission choices [33]. website may want to enforce access control of its own, e.g., by treating an agents read of password field differently from its read of news articles text. Prior defenses likewise assume such representation or fine-grained control over the page. ceLLMate assumes that each website publishes map from its HTTP requests to their meaning [54], UCM has the site owner or an LLM label the regions that hold untrusted content [44], and Prismata has an LLM infer which kind of party authored each element [45]. Websites, however, do not provide such representation, and it cannot be authored in advance, because third-party scripts create and modify elements at runtime (5.2). GENTREE generates this representation at runtime, and we envision extending it with new labels and policies to serve these stakeholders. Conclusion. AI agents increasingly interface with the web on users behalf, yet they read webpages through views that discard web semantics. Securing the web has taken decades of work on origins, isolation, and sanitization. The central lesson of that work is that what content can do must depend on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Agents set this lesson aside when they flatten page into text or pixels and rely on the LLMs judgment. INTACT suggests that the lesson carries over to agents. The browser already knows what each element can do and, with modest 15 instrumentation, who wrote it. An agent that inherits this knowledge can contain attacks that persuade its LLM. Its LLM can also work with far less context for each decision than agents receive today. We believe that agents should treat web semantics as their security boundary, extend these semantics where agents need more, as GENTREE does with provenance, and leave to the LLM only the judgments that the semantics cannot make. Like securing the web itself, securing agents will be long journey. We release INTACTs source code and our attack benchmark of real webpages as foundation for its next steps.

DOM-MUTATE Local change The affected nodes, text, attributes, and covered control state can be restored from sufficient prior state. Recreating markup alone does not restore all application state. APPLY-STYLE Local change Previous declarations and stylesheet configuration can be reinstated. Resource requests and other consequences of applying the style are classified separately. STORAGE-WRITE Local change The prior stored value or absence can be restored with the required metadata and access. This does not retract values already observed or transmitted. SEND-REQUEST External effect transmitted request cannot be withdrawn from its recipient. later compensating operation does not erase the original communication. FETCH External effect Resource retrieval can communicate externally. Once sent, the request cannot be recalled; this label-level rule does not distinguish cache-only retrieval. EXTERNALHANDLER SUBMIT External effect Undetermined The destination or control is handed outside the browsers restoration boundary. The browser has no general means to retract the handoff or restore the external applications state. Submission can cause local change, such as closing dialog, or transmit data. The label alone does not establish its consequences; resulting request is classified separately. NAVIGATE Undetermined Following destination can change local fragment or load another document and communicate externally. The label alone does not establish local inverse. EXECUTE Undetermined Script execution can remain local or cause additional state changes and communication. Running code does not identify or bound its consequences. POST-MESSAGE Undetermined NAVIGATE-FRAME Undetermined The label does not establish whether the recipient is within controlled restoration boundary. delivered message outside that boundary cannot be retracted; the label alone leaves restorability unresolved. Changing frames location or document may be local or involve document replacement and communication. Restorability depends on recoverable document state and the navigation context. RENDER-FRAME Undetermined An embedded document may be generated locally or load resources and run code. Removing it does not establish that its consequences have been undone. External effect identifies communication or handoff beyond that state. Undetermined leaves these consequences unresolved. Interactions receive no category annotation.
